name: White's electric comb

card.summary: A 1920s battery-powered comb marketed to thicken hair and treat scalp problems by passing mild electrical current through the scalp.
card.aka: Electric comb c.1925, Whites electric comb
card.note: A historical device; museum catalogues describe such 'pseudo-medical' devices as of dubious medical worth.

quick.overview:
White's Electric Comb was a 1920s battery-operated comb made in London by Whites Manufacturing Co Ltd. It was sold on the idea that electricity applied to the scalp stimulates the roots and encourages thicker hair, and was used to try to prevent or reverse baldness.

It belongs to a family of early twentieth-century electrical hair devices, including glass-comb electrodes used with high-frequency 'violet ray' sets. No clinical studies of White's comb are known; museums describe it as a pseudo-medical device.
quick.how: The comb was supplied in a box with a directions sheet, and the user applied it to the scalp through combing [1].
quick.risks: No specific safety information about this comb is recorded in the museum catalogues. Museum notes on similar violet-ray devices say they produced a tingling sensation [2].

lead: White's Electric Comb is a metal, battery-powered comb made in England by Whites Manufacturing Co Ltd around 1920 to 1925. Surviving examples carry the markings 'White's electric comb. Made in England' and a patent number on the handle [1]. It was sold to stimulate hair growth and treat scalp problems by applying mild electrical current to the scalp [1].

The appeal was straightforward for the hair-conscious user: comb regularly so that mild electricity stimulates the scalp and, it was claimed, the hair roots. Similar electrical combs and glass 'violet ray' comb electrodes were presented as cures for baldness in the first half of the twentieth century [2]. Museum entries describe these sets as popular home remedies of dubious medical worth [2].

chain: Battery comb applied to scalp daily
Claimed stronger roots and thicker hair
angle.text: Users combed their hair daily with the device in the belief that the mild current would invigorate the roots and produce thicker hair and fewer bald areas. The benefit is as claimed by the maker's instructions.

infobox: Stimulate hair growth, treat scalp problems [1]

paras: A surviving example in the Busselton Historical Society collection (Western Australia) is a metal comb in a crocodile-pattern box with a foam insert and an instruction sheet titled 'Directions for using White's Electric Comb' [1]. The collection record classifies it as a 1920s pseudo-medical device, battery operated, that applied mild electrical currents to the scalp [1].

The violet ray, a high-frequency electrical therapy developed in the 1890s, used glass vacuum electrodes, including comb-shaped ones used on the scalp as a supposed cure for baldness. Science Museum Group catalogue notes say users believed skin stimulation with the sparks relieved pain and promoted hair growth, and call such sets of dubious medical worth [2].
